blocks.text: In thin-layer chromatography (TLC), alumina (Al2O3) or silica (SiO2) is mixed with water to make a slurry, which is spread evenly on a glass slide and dried in an oven to give a white solid layer, the stationary phase. TLC is faster than paper chromatography.

items: A straight baseline is drawn in pencil near the bottom of the slide, and a spot of sample is put on it with a capillary tube; several samples can be spotted side by side.
The solvent is placed in a chromatography tank and the slide is dipped in it (the mobile phase) so that the baseline is above the solvent level.

The components dissolve in the solvent and are adsorbed onto the alumina to different extents. Polar substances are attracted more strongly to the polar solid and travel more slowly; non-polar substances are more soluble in a non-polar solvent and move further up. This separates them.

When the solvent has risen far enough the slide is removed, the solvent front is marked and the slide is dried. Rf values of the spots are calculated and compared with standard values to identify the components.
Colourless components are made visible with a locating agent: ninhydrin turns amino acids purple, some substances glow under ultraviolet light, and some turn brown with iodine vapour.

blocks.alt: Left: two tanks, a TLC plate at the start with two sample spots on the baseline above the solvent, and the same plate after about 10 minutes with each sample separated into three spots below the dashed solvent front. Right: the Quick Check chromatogram of hair dyes, A with one low spot, B with one high spot and C with two spots level with those of A and B.
blocks.caption: Thin-layer chromatography and the hair-dye chromatogram (original diagram after Figure 28.4 and Quick Check 28.1).
blocks.long_description: The solvent rises through the thin layer of silica or alumina and carries each component a different distance. Comparing spots at the same height on one plate shows which substances are the same: a spot from a mixture that matches the height of a pure sample is likely to be that substance.

items: Identifying unknown compounds by comparing their Rf values with standard known values.
Checking the purity of a substance.
Following the progress of a reaction: whether reactants are used up and products made.
In the pharmaceutical and food industries: the purity of drugs and the presence of preservatives, colourants and sweeteners in food.
Detecting pollutants, pesticides and toxic substances in soil, water, food and air.
In forensic science: identifying drugs, post-blast debris, blood, sweat and semen at a crime scene.
It is mainly qualitative: it gives only an idea of the amount of a substance, not an accurate, precise measurement.
It cannot clearly separate compounds with close Rf values, so spots are not always sharp.
Only small amounts of sample can be applied; it is not suitable for large-scale separation.
It is sensitive to humidity, temperature and the cleanliness of the working environment, which reduces reproducibility.
How could a mixture of butanone and pentane be separated by TLC with aluminium oxide as the stationary phase and benzene as the solvent?
In a TLC analysis substance X has a larger Rf value than substance Y. Suggest why.
